chapter.title: Follow the Sun
chapter.sub: A ticket crossed three desks in three time zones. Everyone touched it; nobody owned it; the customer waited for a nine o'clock call.

items.text: SEASON 7 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT  Three desks, three time zones · Maya, Yuki, Sam and Adaeze · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  A boardroom ticket crossed three service desks in three time zones. Everyone touched it. Nobody owned it. The CEO’s assistant waited for a nine o’clock call.  ⚑ RV-151: times illustrative; Tahvara is UTC+8, Valmera UTC+1, Harrowmere UTC−5, none observing daylight saving. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Follow the Sun
items.stakes: Three desks touched one ticket. Nobody owned it. The CEO's assistant waited for a call that was booked thirteen hours late.
items.clock: Before the board meets — Thursday 10:00 Tahvara, 21:00 Wednesday in Harrowmere.
items.reward: A panel that dials — and handovers that can't lose a problem.

objectives.text: Decide how the fix gets done in time
Decide how handovers work from now on
Look closer: two things in the ticket

items.sub: Tuesday · 9:40 p.m. Harrowmere · Wednesday 10:40 a.m. Tahvara

items.alt: The Harrowmere operations centre at night; clocks read 21:40, 03:40 and 10:40. Yuki on the phone with Tahvara; Maya beside her.

bubbles.text: The CEO's assistant. She waited at nine for our test call. Nobody rang.

items.caption: The board meets in Tahvara at ten tomorrow.

items.where: Harrowmere operations centre · Tuesday 21:40 (Wednesday 10:40 in Tahvara)

lines.text: She waited on the line at nine. Their nine. Nobody rang.
Then that's the first thing we fix: somebody's name on it. Mine, for now.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #65 · AVERY'S LENS  Say whose time it is  Every time that crosses a border carries its zone. ‘9:00’ alone is three different moments in a follow-the-sun desk.  The note said ‘test call at 9’. Tahvara meant its morning; Harrowmere read its own. The CEO's assistant waited for a call scheduled thirteen hours later.

items.alt: A ticket card on the wall: opened 16:40, handed to Valmera with ‘test call at 9’, status ‘Awaiting customer’ with 20 minutes of SLA used, handed to Harrowmere with ‘we'll call at 9’; owner: a desk, not a person.
items.caption: Three desks. One note. No name.

items.prompt: 21:50 Harrowmere. The board meets in 28 hours, Tahvara time. Who owns this ticket right now?
items.happening: Ticket open 18 h; test call missed.
items.risk: A board meeting that can't start its call.
timeout: Yuki logs it for the morning desk.
The morning desk reads ‘Harrowmere will call’.

hints.text: Who, by name, is holding this right now?

options.label: The Tahvara desk — it's their region; they'll see it in the morning
options.result: Tahvara's morning desk reads ‘Harrowmere will call’ and waits.

options.label: You do, by name, until it's fixed — you tell the assistant, read every time in the ticket into UTC, and get Sam's desk on the fault tonight
options.result: The assistant has a name; the times line up; Sam's desk finds the fault within the hour.
options.consequence: A person, one clock, the room's owner on the fault.

options.label: Close it and reopen it as a P1 to reset the clock
options.result: The SLA looks fresh; the assistant is still waiting.
options.consequence: Fixing the number, not the problem.

items.title: Whose nine o'clock?
items.body: The Tahvara tech wrote ‘test call at 9’ and meant 09:00 in Tahvara — 01:00 UTC. The Harrowmere desk read its own 09:00 — 14:00 UTC — thirteen hours later, and noted ‘we'll call at 9’. Tahvara's morning desk read that as Harrowmere owning the call. At 01:00 UTC the assistant waited alone.
items.label: Test: how far apart were the two nines — and when does the board meet in Harrowmere?

items.alt: A timeline of Wednesday in UTC: a purple mark at 01:00 UTC labelled 09:00 Tahvara, what the customer meant; a red mark at 14:00 UTC labelled 09:00 Harrowmere, what the desk booked; thirteen hours apart; the SLA paused at 20 minutes while the customer waited 18 hours.
items.caption: Thirteen hours between two nines.

items.prompt: I'm the NOC, not the service desk. Is this even mine to chase?

options.label: “It's yours until someone else says ‘I have it’ and reads it back. That's the rule we're writing tonight.”
options.reply: Then I have it. Until Sam's engineer says so.

options.label: “Not really. Log it for the morning.”
options.reply: That's what the last three desks did.

options.label: “What would you need to own it?”
options.reply: A name to hand it to at the other end. And times I can't misread.

items.title: Awaiting customer
items.body: The status history: 17:00 UTC+8 ‘Awaiting customer’ — set by the Tahvara tech at handover so the SLA wouldn't breach overnight. ‘Standard practice,’ says the desk guide. The customer was waiting for us.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Yuki beside a board. The note says ‘test call at nine’. It was written in Tahvara. Whose nine is it? Tahvara's — UTC plus eight. So one in the morning UTC… which was eight o'clock last night, here. While the note sat in our queue waiting for nine this morning. Every time in UTC, with the customer's local time beside it.

items.caption: Advanced: the formula is there if you ask. Try without it first.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Follow the sun   UTC   Handover note   SLA clock   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Local time from UTC   ƒ FORMULA · Local time from UTC  t local  = t UTC  + offset   t UTC   the time in Coordinated Universal Time  offset  the zone's offset from UTC, hours (negative west of Greenwich)  t local   local clock time — add or subtract 24 h, and change the date, if it crosses midnight      ƒ Ask for the formula · Difference   ƒ FORMULA · Difference  Δ = A − B   A  the larger value  B  the smaller value

items.label: **Learn it now:** follow the sun, handovers and UTC.

items.title: The stopped clock.
items.body: At the 17:00 handover the Tahvara tech set the ticket to ‘Awaiting customer’ — the desk guide's standard move before an overnight gap. It paused the SLA at 20 minutes. For the next seventeen hours and forty minutes the dashboard showed green while the customer waited for a call we owed her.
items.label: Test: how long was the clock paused — and who was really waiting?
**Sequence it:** a handover that survives three time zones.

items.prompt: 23:00 Harrowmere. The panel dials an old directory address. The board meets at 10:00 Tahvara — 21:00 tomorrow here. How does the fix happen in time?
items.clock: Tuesday 23:00 H · Wednesday 12:00 T · board in 22 h
unknown: Whether the new address works from the panel
items.risk: A board meeting on a panel that can't dial.
timeout: The engineer arrives with no tested fix.

hints.text: Who changes that room — and when is ‘nine’ for everyone?

options.label: Change the panel's configuration remotely yourself, now
options.result: Sam: “That's my desk's room. And my engineer's there at eight.”

options.label: Valmera tests the corrected address on a lab panel overnight; Sam's engineer applies it in the room at 08:00 Tahvara; the test call is booked as ‘09:00 UTC+8 · 01:00 UTC · 20:00 Harrowmere (Wed)’ with you on the line
options.result: Applied at 08:10; at 09:00 Tahvara the panel starts the call first time.
options.consequence: Tested where it's safe, applied by the owner, timed in every zone.

options.label: Ask the CEO to run the board meeting from a laptop
options.result: It works — and the room stays broken for the next meeting.
options.consequence: A workaround in place of a fix.

items.title: Railway time
items.body: Until the 1880s most towns kept their own local time by the sun, so railway timetables juggled dozens of ‘noons’. On 18 November 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada switched to a handful of standard time zones; in 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the prime meridian. Trains could finally agree on what ‘9 o'clock’ meant — by saying whose.

items.alt: Wednesday 20:00 in Harrowmere, 09:00 Thursday in Tahvara: Maya on the test call; Sam on screen from the Tahvara boardroom.

bubbles.text: Nine o'clock your time. I'm here.
The panel dialled first time. The assistant says thank you — in two languages.

items.title: old address
items.body: Last month's notice from Tahvara HQ's IT: ‘Directory server moving to a new address on the 3rd.’ The distribution list included every desk — except the room-panel configurations, which still pointed at the old one.

items.alt: The same UTC timeline after the fix: the test call booked as 09:00 UTC+8, 01:00 UTC, 20:00 Harrowmere Wednesday; owner Maya; status ‘Awaiting us’; read back by Sam's desk.
items.caption: One time, written three ways.

items.prompt: Friday. How do handovers work from now on?
items.happening: Board meeting ran; the template hasn't changed.
items.risk: The next ticket lost between desks.
timeout: The template stays as it was.
Next week a Valmera ticket crosses three desks unowned.

hints.text: What would have made ‘9’ impossible to misread — and the owner impossible to miss?

options.label: Every desk works in Harrowmere time
options.result: Tahvara's customers are told ‘21:00’ for their morning.
options.consequence: One clock for us, confusion for everyone else.

options.label: The handover template has a named owner (a person), the state, the evidence, the next action and every time in UTC with the customer's local time; P1/P2 handovers are read back live; ‘Awaiting customer’ is only for when we really are
options.result: Sam's desk adopts it the same week. Valmera adds a column for the customer's language.
options.consequence: Owned, zoned, read back — and honest statuses.

options.label: Drop follow-the-sun; one desk, 24 hours
options.result: Night shifts in one country, forever.

options.label: Add a fourth desk
options.result: Four handovers a day instead of three.

items.alt: Friday evening handover in the operations centre; clocks read 17:00, 23:00 and 06:00. Yuki reads a note aloud to the Tahvara desk.

bubbles.text: …next action, test call, oh-one-hundred UTC, oh-nine-hundred yours. Owner: Priti. Read it back?
That's the whole trick. Say it twice, in their time.

items.alt: Valmera's new training centre; Luis on the phone, frustrated, in front of a blank front display.

bubbles.text: My training rooms die for eight minutes every hour. Your dashboard says a hundred percent uptime.
Every hour? At the same minute?

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Local time = UTC + offset. Every time that crosses a desk carries its zone — write the UTC time with the customer’s local time beside it. A handover names a person, the state, the evidence and the next action with its due time, and is read back. A status that pauses the clock must say who is really waiting.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Think of the last time you handed something over. Could the next person have known, without asking, exactly what to do and by when?
